One-line judgment: this line of work is not about pulling network cables or configuring switches, but about designing and implementing data communication networks such as local area networks (LAN) and wide area networks (WAN) and intranets and extranets, doing capacity modeling and analysis, and possibly designing security measures and recommending hardware and software. The work of computer network architects can be divided into three linked but independent work dimensions. The first is requirements and current state and capacity planning: extract requirements from business services and traffic and availability and latency and compliance and recovery targets; draw the current-state topology and trust boundaries; monitor and analyze network performance and input and output reports to find problems, identify inefficient use of computer resources or do capacity planning; adjust network scale to meet traffic or capacity needs; and determine specific network hardware or software requirements, such as platform and interfaces and bandwidth or conventional patterns. The second is network and security design: develop disaster recovery plans; develop or recommend network security measures such as firewalls and network security audits or automated security detection; design, build or run device configuration prototypes, including network hardware and software and servers or server operating systems; develop conceptual, logical or physical network designs; and evaluate network designs to judge whether they meet customer needs efficiently and effectively. The third is delivery and operations and collaboration: develop and implement solutions to network problems; maintain the network through activities such as adding and removing files or backups; coordinate network operations and maintenance and repair or upgrades; coordinate new equipment installation; participate in network technology upgrade or expansion projects, including hardware and software installation and integration testing; write network-related documentation and installation and usage and troubleshooting procedures; prepare detailed network specifications, including diagrams and tables and equipment configurations or recommended technologies; communicate with users to confirm that accounts are set up correctly or to diagnose and resolve operational problems; communicate with suppliers to obtain product information and forecast demand or resolve problems; estimate the time and materials needed to complete projects; and instruct engineers or other staff in designing or implementing network solutions.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether requirements and availability and recovery targets are written to a verifiable level; whether the current state and dependencies and trust boundaries are fully mapped; whether capacity and failure domains have measured and assumed basis; whether security and access policies meet least-privilege and compliance requirements; whether changes are phased and have validation and rollback and stop conditions; and whether configuration and topology and test and rollback evidence is kept on record.
Judgment one: whether requirements and availability and recovery targets are written to a verifiable level

Turn business services and traffic and latency and availability and recovery targets into measurable metrics (bandwidth and concurrency and latency and packet loss and recovery time objectives); for parts that cannot be quantified, state the assumptions and the verification method; do not replace acceptance conditions with scope-free wording such as the network being faster and more stable.
Judgment two: whether the current state and dependencies and trust boundaries are fully mapped

Draw the current-state topology and traffic paths and service dependencies and mark the trust boundaries; explicitly write out unmanaged devices and shadow links and legacy configurations and assess the risk; confirm redundancy and failure impact for critical dependencies.
Judgment three: whether capacity and failure domains have measured and assumed basis

Build a capacity baseline from monitoring and stress testing and historical peaks and write down the assumptions; clarify single points of failure and the failure domain scope and convergence time; mark uncertainty and a re-test plan for projections beyond the measured range.
Judgment four: whether security and access policies meet least-privilege and compliance requirements

Design access policies according to least privilege and zone isolation and keep the basis for the rules; confirm authorization and audit requirements for remote and out-of-band access and account and credential management; bring changes to security measures into the same change and rollback process.
Judgment five: whether changes are phased and have validation and rollback and stop conditions

Validate in a lab or isolated environment before releasing in phases; define validation metrics and rollback trigger conditions and responsible persons for each step; clarify stop conditions and the escalation path, and do not continue executing while a fault is expanding.
Judgment six: whether configuration and topology and test and rollback evidence is kept on record

Archive topology and configuration and version and drift records and test results and rollback and subsequent reviews; set up detection and comparison for configuration drift over time; enable others to restore to the pre-change state from the records.

The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: reading topology and protocols, speaking with monitoring and traffic data, executing according to change processes, and keeping configuration and records. The real difference lies in the scope of responsibility: this occupation is responsible for end-to-end topology and capacity and evolution; the management direction focuses on people and budget and delivery; the systems analysis direction focuses on business solutions; the security direction focuses on monitoring and controls; the network support and computer support directions focus on day-to-day faults and user support; the operations and maintenance direction focuses on equipment and protocol execution and inspections. When choosing, it is suggested to first verify with a deliverable exercise of requirements and targets — current state and capacity — design and validation and rollback, rather than comparing titles first.

The comparison is based on the occupational definition and 33 tasks and work activities and work context descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 15-1241.00 page, the related and adjacent occupation codes listed there, the adjacent occupation slug list registered in this evidence route (computer-and-information-systems-managers, computer-systems-analysts, information-security-analysts, computer-network-support-specialists, computer-support-specialists), and public occupational materials for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is editorial synthesis and does not constitute a cybersecurity, compliance or legal conclusion.

The table below compares roles and occupations adjacent to this occupation: computer and information systems managers, computer systems analysts, information security analysts, computer network support specialists, computer support specialists, and the network operations and maintenance direction. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Computer and information systems managers focus on people, budget, project and delivery coordination, and may also take part in technical architecture; network architects focus on topology, capacity and evolution.
People willing to coordinate department people and budget and delivery suit that direction; people willing to do network design and capacity planning suit this occupation.
Mainly department plans and budgets and project delivery and operations records.
Computer and information systems managers

Computer systems analysts focus on translating business requirements into system solutions and coordinating them, and usually do not carry network capacity and failure domain responsibility; this occupation takes verifiable network metrics as its object.
People willing to do requirements analysis and solution coordination suit that direction; people willing to do network design and validation suit this occupation.
Mainly requirements and solutions and implementation coordination records.
Computer systems analysts

Information security analysts focus on security monitoring and incident analysis and controls, and usually are not responsible for overall network capacity and redundancy design; this occupation treats security as part of the design.
People willing to specialize in security monitoring and incident response suit that direction; people willing to coordinate network and security design trade-offs suit this occupation.
Mainly security alerts and incidents and hardening records.
Information security analysts

Computer network support specialists focus on day-to-day fault support and troubleshooting for networks and endpoints, and usually do not carry end-to-end design and capacity planning; this occupation is responsible for topology and evolution.
People willing to do frontline troubleshooting and user support suit that direction; people willing to do design review and change management suit this occupation.
Mainly tickets and troubleshooting and configuration records.
Computer network support specialists

Computer support specialists cover networks and user support, focus on operations troubleshooting services, and may also take part in configuration and upgrades; the difference from architecture work is the center of responsibility, and it cannot be said flatly that they do not involve network security.
People willing to do user and desktop support suit that direction; people willing to do network architecture and capacity planning suit this occupation.
Mainly tickets and equipment and account handling records.
Computer support specialists

Among adjacent occupations, roles related to computer network architecture also include the network and systems administrator and network engineer directions; the former leans toward day-to-day operations and maintenance, the latter toward equipment and protocol implementation; this occupation leans toward end-to-end design, capacity modeling and evolution planning.
People willing to work long-term on equipment and operations maintenance suit the operations direction; people willing to do design and planning suit this occupation.
Mainly operations and maintenance and change and inspection records.
Computer network support specialists

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires adding new capabilities and experience: the management direction needs people and budget and delivery management experience; the systems analysis direction needs business modeling and requirements engineering experience; the security direction needs security monitoring and incident response and hardening experience; the network support direction needs frontline troubleshooting and ticket and user support experience; the computer support direction needs desktop and account and device support experience; the operations and maintenance direction needs equipment and protocol and inspection and upgrade execution experience. Topology and protocol and monitoring capabilities can transfer, but the scope of responsibility and authority of each direction must be re-established.

The five steps below are the editorial process given on this page, used to explain who is responsible at which step; they are not a mandatory process prescribed by a source, nor do they replace the employer's own change and security and configuration management systems.

Clarify requirements and availability targets and trust boundaries, as well as your own authority boundaries and escalation path for production changes and out-of-band access and external communication.

Roles with the corresponding authority and qualifications confirm change and security and compliance conclusions; tools do not carry that responsibility and do not exempt anyone from security and compliance obligations.

Automatically generated configuration or policy suggestions may not match the real device syntax and dependencies; pushing them without validation in an isolated environment will cause outages or exposure.
Base everything only on device documentation and measured topology and monitoring data; validate uncertain points in an isolated environment first and keep the validation process and conclusions.
Topology and configuration and accounts and credentials and traffic logs are protected information, and uploading them to external services may cause leakage and compliance risk.

Missing device model, system version, input configuration or model output version makes change drafts non-reproducible and hides drift.
Record the model, system and input and output versions, original logs and approvals; compare manually and then validate in isolation, and do not rely on alert grouping alone for root cause.
Generated syntax that is incompatible with the device model or system or dependencies may fail to execute or produce incorrect routing policy.
Validate syntax and dependencies in a version-matched isolated environment, check differences and acceptance; do not push without approval, and keep stop and rollback records.

paragraphs: The six cards are editorial risk scenarios and control suggestions based on U.S. O*NET tasks; they are not incident rates, a ranking of the most common risks or a verified mandatory employer procedure; the actual network change, security and authorization texts in the applicable jurisdiction or organization were not obtained this round, and each item must be checked separately.

Editorial judgment: you can first check capacity and dependencies, configuration drift and monitoring, and the impact and recovery conditions of routing / access / DNS / load balancing changes. Outage and exposure are possible consequences, and no ranking of most common or most important risks is given; data and credential confidentiality and handover also need checking.

Evidence scope: tasks and work context come from O*NET 15-1241.00 (U.S. scope); U.S. wages are 2025 data and employment and projections are on the 2025—2035 scope (181,800 → 195,800, growth 7.7%, average annual openings 9,600); Mainland China is two clearly labeled industry average proxies (248,752 / 128,166 yuan / year), not values for this occupation; the security and compliance and authority boundaries are stated according to public systems and general frameworks and do not replace the text of applicable regulations or employer systems.
Roles that carry capacity and dependency analysis

An outdated capacity baseline or a missing dependency or an unidentified single point of failure will make the design fail at peak and during faults, and affect service availability and recovery time.

Build a capacity baseline from monitoring and stress testing and historical peaks and write down the assumptions; review the baseline and dependency changes regularly; clarify single points of failure and failure domain scope and convergence time and keep the analysis records.
Reusing an outdated capacity table; treating uncertain dependencies as known; drawing only the logical topology without marking failure domains and convergence paths.
Roles that carry configuration and change execution
Undocumented configuration drift or manual changes will make the actual network inconsistent with the design, and during a fault it will be impossible to judge the root cause and the rollback point.

Manage configuration with templates and version control and compare drift regularly; review changes through the process and record the scope of impact and the executor; build a list of unmanaged devices and legacy configurations and bring them under management step by step.

Changing production configuration directly without authorization or validation, not recording changes, and leaving temporary changes with no plan for removal are the risky behaviors this page's editorial note flags; actual production changes may be carried out under the organization's approved procedures.
Roles that carry security and access policy design
A wrong routing or access policy or DNS or load balancing change can cause widespread outage, or cause data and service exposure and compliance liability.

Design access policies according to least privilege and zone isolation and keep the basis for the rules; confirm authorization and audit requirements for remote and out-of-band access and account and credential management; validate in an isolated environment, then release in phases with rollback and stop conditions prepared.
Opening policy temporarily for convenience with no plan to remove it; sharing administrator accounts; changing the backbone without a change window and without out-of-band access prepared.
Roles that carry monitoring and fault response
Monitoring blind spots or excessive alert noise will delay detection and localization of faults, and let the scope of impact grow before it is found.

Cover key metrics and synthetic probes by service and failure domain and define alert thresholds; check blind spots and alert effectiveness regularly; keep incident timelines and handling and post-incident records and track corrective actions to closure.
Monitoring only device ports and not services; letting alerts pile up unhandled; not doing post-incident review or corrective action tracking after a fault.
Roles that carry data and credential and configuration confidentiality
Leakage of topology and configuration and credentials and traffic logs lowers the cost of attack and creates compliance and customer trust risk.

Manage according to credential type, organizational policy and leak risk; on leakage, revoke or rotate immediately, without requiring that all passwords be forcibly changed periodically. Exporting or sending topology, configuration or logs must be authorized and desensitized and recorded, and third-party access must have clear boundaries.

Uploading topology and configuration without authorization, failing to revoke credentials after a leak, and sending logs out without desensitization must all be stopped and reported according to the actual process.
Roles that carry design and change handover
Designs and changes that are not recorded or not synchronized to the operations and security teams will cause handover gaps and conflicts with later changes.

Write topology and design notes and configuration versions and tests and rollback and known issues into handover materials; update the design and monitoring and documentation after changes; keep records of post-handover support and training.
Handing over verbally only; documentation inconsistent with configuration versions; not updating the design and monitoring baseline after release.

subject.name: Computer network architect
subject.summary: Design and implement data communication networks such as local area networks (LAN) and wide area networks (WAN) and intranets and extranets, perform network modeling, analysis and planning, including analysis of network infrastructure capacity requirements, may also design network and computer security measures, and research and recommend network and data communications hardware and software: develop disaster recovery plans; develop or recommend security measures such as firewalls and security audits or automated security detection; develop and implement solutions to network problems; maintain the network and coordinate operations and maintenance and upgrades; monitor and analyze network performance and do capacity planning; design conceptual and logical and physical networks and build configuration prototypes; write network documentation and installation and usage and troubleshooting procedures and specifications; communicate with users and suppliers and customers; estimate time and materials; and instruct engineers or other staff.
